title: The Dodgers Before The Machine
contentHtml:
Monday night brought with it a formality that was nonetheless historic in its own right: the Los Angeles Dodgers officially clinched a spot in the 2026 MLB playoffs, marking the 14th consecutive season that L.A. is headed for postseason play. That ties the 1991-2005 Atlanta Braves for the longest such streak in history — and those Braves come with the asterisk that their playoff fate was not fully assured in 1994 at the time play ceased.1

The longest postseason streaks

The Dodgers have also won three times as many World Series in that span as the Braves did in theirs, and they’re market favorites (if not odds-on favorites) to tie the Yankees’ 1990s/2000s dynasty at four titles apiece if they cash in this October. There’s a growing case to be made for these Dodgers as one of the absolute top dynasties in baseball history, especially if they keep winning this season.

But things weren’t always so sunny in Hollywood. Hard as it is to believe now, there was (by definition) a time when the Dodgers didn’t make the playoffs every year. In fact, they missed the playoffs three straight years (2010-2012) leading up to the current streak, and before a couple of NLCS runs in 2008-09, they had a single playoff win in the previous 19 years — dating back to right after 1988, with Kirk Gibson’s HR and all that.

How did the Dodgers go from that — a big-market franchise that could certainly produce stars, but still routinely fielded unspectacular teams around them, struggling to make the playoffs — to this, where October is basically assumed before the season even begins?
